beats.name: Ole Romer
beats.role: Danish astronomer at the Royal Observatory in Paris

beats.text: Romer noticed that eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io ran early when Earth was closest to Jupiter, and late when it was furthest away.
beats.note: The gap was not Io's orbit changing: it was extra light needing extra distance to cross. Most scientists at the time assumed light travelled instantly.

beats.context: how long Romer calculated light takes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit around the Sun.

beats.text: His figures imply a speed of about 226,663 kilometres per second: roughly 24% slower than the true value of 299,792 km/s.
beats.note: He was off by a quarter. He was also the first person in history to prove light has a speed at all.

beats.text: Giovanni Cassini, the observatory's own director and the astronomer whose data Romer had used, never fully accepted the theory.
beats.note: It won support elsewhere in Europe well before Paris came around to it.

beats.line: He measured the speed of light in 1676 by watching a moon of Jupiter.
